comparator.route: Economic History focus area with minor and internship
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 Dutch ESHCC regulations control (article 10.3); Appendix 9 confirms the complete 180-EC History pathway. Preserve eight first-year courses (60 EC), three required second-year theory/method courses (22.5 EC), one complete 30-EC focus area, one 7.5-EC elective, 22.5 EC of thesis class/thesis and one 37.5-EC third-year option. Economic History and option 1 with internship remain the first-listed choices, independently of UCR fit. The elective and minor remain approved choice categories, without inventing subjects. Positive first-year study advice requires all 60 EC after permitted compensation (article 9.1); BA-2/3 exams require positive advice, subject to the article 4.3 personal-circumstances exception. The internship requires completed BA-1 and must be field-specific, normally in BA-3 term 2, completed within six consecutive months. Thesis-class entry requires completed BA-1 and at least 45 EC in BA-2/3 including three focus-area courses (22.5 EC); that class must be passed before submitting the thesis. The ordinary minor requires third-year registration and selection from the admission matrix. The 15-EC honours programme is extracurricular and excluded. Lectures are English, BA-1 practicals Dutch, later practicals Dutch/English; assessment may require English if the examiner does not master Dutch, and the GS thesis is written in Dutch. Marketing statements about all assessment being Dutch do not override article 3.3. The programme page uses a different philosophy-course code, but the formal title and 7.5 EC agree; no uncertain code is encoded.

How can primary sources, data and historical representation be analysed critically?

alternatives.concept: A historically anchored programme combines all six available UCR History courses with three art-history courses on Renaissance-to-modern visual culture, early-modern global connections and historiography. Economics, sociology, political thought and international relations supply complementary explanations of institutions, inequality and change; quantitative and qualitative methods support inquiry. The final History seminar researches primary sources from the 1809 Walcheren Expedition. This is sustained historical study, but it does not reproduce Erasmus’s complete economic-history focus area, philosophy-of-history course, individual thesis or internship.

alternatives.concept: A historical programme centres all six UCR History courses, with historically grounded work on human rights, political thought and race in media. International-relations theory, comparative politics, peace and conflict, international and EU law, EU politics and social theory provide complementary tools for studying international order and power. The six-course History sequence and archival research supply the historical anchor; the law and politics courses do not become specialised diplomatic-history courses through this combination.

alternatives.labelRationale: The route retains all six UCR History courses while concentrating its adjacent work in comparative politics, international relations, conflict, international and EU law, institutions and global governance. alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Relative to the closest programme, nine courses (67.5 EC) differ in each programme. The international option replaces five economics courses, introductory sociology and three art-history courses with a law gateway, human rights, international/constitutional/EU law, EU politics, peace and conflict, race in media and community-engaged rhetoric. It preserves the historical spine but changes its complementary question from economy and society to international order and conflict.

alternatives.concept: A social and cultural history programme combines all six UCR History courses with art history, Renaissance connections, African heritage, museums, archaeology and historiography. Social theory, movements, qualitative methods, literature, film, race in media and documentary analysis extend its study of historical experience and representation. Ancient archaeology and literary/media methods supply distinct evidence and perspectives; they do not replace Erasmus’s modern-history and disciplinary-method requirements.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Modern History, introductory economics and sociology begin in semester 1. Research Methods & Statistics precedes all five formally dependent economics courses. The thematic History courses precede the final archival-source seminar. Art history and political thought in semester 5 support final historiography and early-modern global art study; qualitative methods and social theory complement the historical work. The final-year art courses are placed in their actually marked terms. All formal prerequisites, offerings and advanced-course rules were checked placement by placement.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest programme owns the broad historical identity, inquiry and past-present themes with a direct historical sequence strengthened by Renaissance art and historiography; its five economics courses are complementary support for the selected external economic-history route, not a claim to reproduce that focus area. The international option follows explicit political/conflict and International Relations interests; the social-cultural option follows explicit social/cultural interests and the coherent overlap of two formal focus areas. Teaching is separately rejected: primary-school rhetorical engagement does not supply history pedagogy, secondary-school placement or teacher qualification. All generator interests have a core owner or coherent candidate; no outcome-only interest generates an alternative. Distinctness is qualitative and exceeds the four-course/30-EC floor in all pairs (9, 9 and 11 courses). Three is the maximum reached after evidence, comparability and feasibility checks, not a target.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both substantively survey nineteenth- and twentieth-century political, economic and cultural change, including industrial societies, international power, crises and the welfare state. UCR begins in 1815 and extends to the present.

Both involve advanced historical primary-source inquiry and a substantial research paper. UCR researches the 1809 Walcheren Expedition; Erasmus prepares a separate Economic History thesis. The UCR seminar does not deliver that focus-area thesis.

No single scheduled UCR course provides the external global survey from 1500 across Western and non-Western societies. Modern History is more strongly aligned to Global Societies, and the thematic History courses supply narrower studies.
Primary-source work is present in the advanced History Research Seminar, already aligned to the thesis class. There is no separately scheduled introductory historian-training course.
Past-present connections run through the programme, but no course directly delivers the external introductory historiography/relevance course.

Native American and gender histories offer substantial other historical studies, but none of the scheduled courses directly examines the Netherlands’ history and global position from the Middle Ages onward.
General rhetoric and PPD support academic writing, but do not require the external 4,000-word historical paper. The advanced primary-source seminar has a stronger relationship to the thesis class.
Art historiography is substantive but is not the external general philosophy-of-history course covering its central intellectual traditions.
The approved 7.5-EC elective subject remains unspecified; no single UCR course is asserted as its counterpart.
The external 15-EC individual thesis is compulsory. No scheduled UCR course is a bachelor thesis; optional independent research is displayed alongside it outside the UCR 180 EC.
Both teach research design and quantitative/statistical analysis of empirical data. UCR provides general research/statistics training; Erasmus applies it specifically to historical data.

Both teach qualitative research design, interpretation and analysis of evidence. UCR undertakes general social-research projects; Erasmus specifically develops historical-source methods such as oral history, narrative and discourse analysis.
The approved 15-EC minor is a choice category, not one scheduled UCR course.
PPD and primary-school rhetoric are complementary skills/community engagement, not a course on historians’ professional and societal practice.
The selected 15-EC field-specific internship is not delivered by any scheduled UCR course.

Both directly examine economic inequality and the relation of institutions/policy to distribution. UCR focuses on economic models and evidence about taxation, spending and redistribution; Erasmus investigates capitalism and inequality historically.
No scheduled UCR course directly studies historical relationships between multinationals and nation-states. General organisational psychology has been withdrawn and is not an adequate counterpart.
Introductory economics supplies analytical context but does not teach the external historical cases of emerging economies and global labour. Keep this component separate.

Both substantively introduce international-relations theories and apply them through historical and contemporary cases. Erasmus specifically connects this field to economic globalisation since the nineteenth century; UCR’s scope is broader international relations.
Both introduce sociological concepts and theories and their social-historical context. Erasmus explicitly applies them to historical research; UCR is a broader introductory sociology course.

Both study early-modern cross-cultural encounters and the Renaissance. UCR focuses on Italian art and its Mediterranean/global connections through trade and colonisation, rather than the external course’s broader early-modern social history.

notes.text: Erasmus provides a continuous History degree with disciplinary methods, philosophy of history, a complete focus area, a compulsory individual thesis and a structured third-year route. The UCR programmes retain a six-course History spine and build distinct interdisciplinary directions around it. They support substantial historical inquiry but leave gaps in chronology, Dutch history, the selected economic-history specialisation and professional practice. General economics, law, rhetoric and social-science courses remain complementary. Optional independent research is additional to the scheduled 180 EC and is not a guaranteed replacement for Erasmus’s thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: History at Erasmus studies social, cultural, economic and political change from 1500, with particular attention to the last two centuries and questions about society today. Students learn to work with historical sources, choose a focus area and complete a thesis. This comparison shows Economic History with a minor and a field-specific internship. The degree is the Dutch History track: lectures are English, first-year practicals are Dutch, and later teaching and assessment can use both languages under the programme rules.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Each UCR option combines all six available History courses with a different set of supporting fields. The closest option adds economics, social analysis, art history and historiography; the other options emphasise international order or social and cultural representation. These are substantial interdisciplinary historical programmes with different scope from a full History degree. They do not reproduce Erasmus’s complete economic-history focus area, required individual thesis or internship. A shared row means a meaningful partial relationship; blank cells identify other content or a gap.
